citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China, Meituan Group)
description: POPE is a Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation benchmark for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about objects in images (e.g., "Is there a car in the image?"). It supports three sampling strategies (Random, Popular, Adversarial) and is built on images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets.
name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image (l=6), with 3 positive (ground-truth objects) and 3 negative (nonexistent objects) questions each.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: POPE constructs binary Yes/No questions using a template "Is there a/an <object> in the image?". Positive questions use ground-truth objects from annotations; negative questions use nonexistent objects sampled via three strategies: (1) Random Sampling — randomly sample objects not in the image; (2) Popular Sampling — select top-k most frequent objects in the dataset not in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling — rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k not in the image. The ratio of positive to negative questions is 1:1.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is designed to expose biases in LVLMs: objects that frequently appear or co-occur in visual instruction datasets (based on MSCOCO) are more likely to be hallucinated. The Popular and Adversarial sampling strategies specifically target these biases by selecting frequently appearing or co-occurring objects as negative samples. The visual instruction datasets used to train LVLMs have an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part.
rai:dataCollection: POPE is built on images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. For MSCOCO-based POPE, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are randomly selected from the validation set. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. Polling questions are constructed by pairing ground-truth objects (positive) with nonexistent objects sampled under Random, Popular, or Adversarial strategies (negative), with a 1:1 ratio.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations from MSCOCO validation set, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. MSCOCO provides human-labeled object annotations and captions; A-OKVQA and GQA images are annotated using the SEEM automatic segmentation tool.
rai:dataLimitations: POPE only focuses on object hallucination and cannot measure overall LVLM performance. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of validation data, so results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers, leading to inaccurate results. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, causing divergence in evaluation results.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Negative object sampling is performed under three strategies: Random (random sampling of absent objects), Popular (top-k most frequent MSCOCO objects absent from the image), and Adversarial (top-k objects most frequently co-occurring with ground-truth objects but absent from the image). The ratio of positive to negative questions is set to 1:1 for label balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images are filtered to include only those with more than 3 ground-truth objects. For MSCOCO, 500 images are randomly selected from the validation set. Object annotations follow the 80 COCO object categories from the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For A-OKVQA and GQA, SEEM is used to generate object annotations from images.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect environmental understanding could make wrong decisions, leading to serious safety issues. The dataset aims to help develop more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs by providing a stable evaluation framework for hallucination.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs); benchmarking LVLM reliability and accuracy in object recognition; comparing hallucination rates across different LVLMs; extending hallucination evaluation to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) — an automatic segmentation tool used to annotate objects in images from A-OKVQA and GQA datasets (and also used as an alternative to human annotations for MSCOCO). ChatGPT is used to parse open-ended VQA responses for evaluation.

evidence.name: we further design a polling-based query method called POPE for better evaluation of object hallucination.
evidence.description: The basic idea is to convert the evaluation of hallucination into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No short questions about the probing objects (e.g., Is there a car in the image?). We show that such a method is more stable and flexible.

evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: We adopt SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) to annotate images from three datasets (i.e., MSCOCO, A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022) and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019)) and build POPE based on the segmentation results.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and construct 6 questions for each image (i.e., l= 6). For computing the CHAIR metric on MSCOCO, we follow the settings in Rohrbach et al. (2018) which only considers 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Random Sampling: we randomly sample the objects that do not exist in the image. Popular Sampling: we select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole image dataset that do not exist in the current image, where k=l/2. Adversarial Sampling: we first rank all objects according to their co-occurring frequencies with the ground-truth objects, and then select the top-k frequent ones that do not exist in the image.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: with the assistance of automatic segmentation tools, POPE can be easily extended to datasets without annotations. To validate it, we adopt SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) to annotate images from three datasets (i.e., MSCOCO, A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022) and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019)) and build POPE based on the segmentation results.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: we further design a polling-based query method called POPE for better evaluation of object hallucination. Experiment results show that our POPE can evaluate object hallucination in a more stable and flexible way.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: our proposed POPE utilizes a matching-based method to determine whether LVLMs answer "Yes" or "No", while empirically, LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide answers explicitly containing these words, which may lead to inaccurate evaluation results. Fourth, when combined with the automatic segmentation tool, the objects would be annotated based on the label set by the tool, which may be inconsistent with the collected human annotations, leading to a divergence in evaluation results.

evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, as it may result in unexpected consequences caused by these hallucinated objects. For example, due to an incorrect understanding of the external environment, an autonomous driving system would make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, which might lead to serious safety issues.
